Abstract 13

We present a method for creating spacecraft-like data which can be used to train 14

Machine Learning (ML) models to detect and classify structures in in-situ spacecraft data. 15

First, we use the Grad-Shafranov (GS) equation to numerically solve for several mag- 16

netohydrostatic equilibria which are variations on a known analytic equilibrium. These 17

equilibria are then used as the initial conditions for Particle-In-Cell (PIC) simulations 18

in which the structures of interest are observed and labeled. We then take one-dimensional 19

slices through the simulations to replicate what a spacecraft collecting data from the sim- 20

ulation would observe. This sliced data then can be used as training data for the initial 21

training of ML models intended for use on spacecraft data. We demonstrate the method 22

applied to the problem of detecting small-scale plasmoids in the magnetotail, which is 23

important for understanding complex magnetotail reconnection dynamics. The simple 24

1D classifier we train is able to detect more than 70% of the plasmoid points in the dataset 25

but also produces a large number of false positives. Our further work on this example 26

problem is detailed, and further potential uses of the method are discussed. 27

1 Introduction 28

In-situ spacecraft data is an important component of space physics research. In- 29

situ instruments that are directly immersed in the local plasma environment are able to 30

measure quantities which are difficult or impossible to obtain via remote measurement. 31

Interpretation of those measured quantities, however, is not straightforward. A satellite 32

instrument collects time series data, meaning it samples the data at discrete points in 33

time. At the same time, the spacecraft may be moving significantly relative to the lo- 34

cal plasma environment; for example, structures entrained in a magnetic reconnection 35

outflow can move past the spacecraft at high speed. Additionally, while a spacecraft may 36

be able to take data at different physical locations on the spacecraft, the spacecraft is 37

generally very small compared to the plasma structures it is taking data from. There- 38

fore, a single spacecraft’s data is a 1D snapshot of the full 4D picture of a three dimen- 39

sional plasma evolving with time. This makes interpretation of spacecraft data difficult 40

despite the high quality of the local measurements. As a consequence, methodologies for 41

analysis of in-situ spacecraft data are sophisticated and varied. For example, there is a 42

wide range of techniques for single and multiple spacecraft that aim to determine the 43

geometry and/or orientation of observed plasma structures (e.g. Sonnerup & Cahill Jr., 44

1967; Paschmann & Daly, 1998; Sonnerup et al., 2006; Shi et al., 2006; Fu et al., 2015; 45

Torbert et al., 2020). Still, however, much existing spacecraft data has difficult or am- 46

biguous interpretation, as existing methods cannot always conclusively determine whether 47

an observed structure is spatial, temporal, or both. 48

As Machine Learning techniques have risen in prominence, there have been a num- 49

ber of successful attempts to apply them to the interpretation and analysis of in-situ space- 50

craft data (e.g. Argall et al., 2020; Breuillard et al., 2020; dos Santos et al., 2020; Gar- 51

ton et al., 2021; Olshevsky et al., 2021). There have been successful attempts to use un- 52

supervised learning for plasma structure identification (Innocenti et al., 2021), but the 53

problem of identifying plasma structures within the data translates naturally to a clas- 54

sification problem, which can be tackled via supervised learning. Since supervised learn- 55

ing requires a training dataset where the ‘correct’ answer is known, attempts to utilize 56

it in the past have either relied on training datasets comprising spacecraft data which 57

has already been classified via a different method (e.g. Argall et al., 2020; Garton et al., 58

2021; Lenouvel et al., 2021) or comprising modeled or simulated data (e.g. dos Santos 59

et al., 2020). Models of the former kind can be particularly useful in reducing workload 60

on researchers in cases where plasma structure identification is done via meticulous vi- 61

sual inspection. In this work we have opted for the latter and developed a framework 62

for training models based on simulated data. This choice allows the models to achieve 63

potentially better performance than existing identification methods, including visual in- 64

spection. 65

There are a number of potential pitfalls to consider when training models on sim- 66

ulated data. The success of a model depends hugely on the quality of its input data. Sim- 67

ulated data has less fluctuations and variability than real space; for example, perfectly 68

flat, uniformly dense current sheets are not found in nature. Care must be taken to en- 69

sure that the simulated input dataset is sufficiently representative of real space, and even 70

then domain adaptation methods such as those described in Singhal et al. (2023) should 71

be considered to optimize performance on real data. In order to tackle this problem, we 72

have developed a method of solving perturbed Grad-Shafranov (GS) equations to cre- 73

ate ‘messy’ magnetostatic equilibria that can be used as initial conditions in Particle- 74

In-Cell (PIC) simulations, and have then taken 1D slices through these perturbed sim- 75

ulations to synthesize an input dataset suitable for training a classification model. We 76

demonstrate this method using the example case of training a 1D Convolutional Neu- 77

ral Network (CNN)-based classifier to identify plasmoids in reconnection regions. Note 78

that this approach is one of many: there are other ways to increase the realism of sim- 79

ulation data, such as applying realistic instrument noise and using the same spatial res- 80

olution as an existing instrument. Such methods have been used with great success by 81

e.g. Tremblay et al. (2018) but they are beyond the scope of this report. 82

1.1 Motivation for our example case: detecting plasmoids in the mag- 83

netotail 84

Earth’s magnetotail is an elongated plasma environment, spanning 20-60 Earth radii 85

(Re) radially in the Y-Z Geocentric Solar Magnetospheric (GSM) plane but up to hun- 86

dreds of Re in the -X GSM direction away from the Sun. The tail is often described in 87

terms of near (∼<20 Re), mid (∼20-60 Re), and far (∼>60 Re) regions, though there 88

are no precise definitions for these terms. Magnetic reconnection in the near-to-mid tail 89

is often bursty, significantly influenced by internal magnetosphere dynamics in addition 90

to direct driving, and allows finite guide fields (Petrukovich et al., 2016). Additionally, 91

near-to-mid-tail reconnection is often associated with dipolarizations during substorms. 92

The complex reconnection situation and the association with global magnetospheric changes 93

makes the phenomenon important to study. 94

Another key feature of interest is the presence of plasmoids – regions with loop- 95

or helix-shaped magnetic field lines – which may have been formed via the plasmoid in- 96

stability. Small-scale plasmoids have been observed in the tail via in-situ measurements 97

many times (e.g. Chen et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2012). If near-to-mid tail reconnection 98

is capable of producing many coexisting small-scale plasmoids, those plasmoids will have 99

a significant impact on reconnection dynamics and energization efficiency in the region. 100

Statistical properties of plasmoid dynamics of reconnecting current sheets are important 101

to quantify multiscale reconnection in large plasmas in general (Ji et al., 2022). 102

Researchers have used a number of methods to detect plasmoids in in-situ data in 103

the past. Automated methods are repeatable, rigorous, and are less susceptible to hu- 104

man bias. For example, there are well-performing methods that automatically detect flux 105

ropes in satellite data (Smith et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018). These two methods can 106

determine valuable information such as the flux rope’s radius. However, both methods 107

fit the spacecraft data to cylindrical flux rope models, force-free (Lundquist, 1950) and 108

non-force-free (Elphic & Russell, 1983) respectively. These methods may not perform 109

optimally in dynamic reconnection regions where large numbers of plasmoids are squashed 110

or deformed from cylindrical shapes and the structure’s magnetic field and the turbu- 111

lent background field are difficult to distinguish from each other. Simpler geometry-based 112

algorithms have also been developed (Bergstedt et al., 2020), but their generality invites 113

the possiblity of large numbers of false positives and they cannot distinguish whether 114

they are detecting a plasmoid or the travelling compression region surrounding it. 115

Researchers will also often rely on their experience to identify plasmoids in data 116

‘by eye’. This approach works well for case studies focused on one or two plasmoids and 117

their nearby environment where all the nuances of the plasma’s characteristics must be 118

understood; in contrast, this approach is a poor choice for statistical studies of many plas- 119

moids due to the method’s inherent subjectivity and excessive consumption of researcher 120

time. There have been numerous groundbreaking case studies which have advanced our 121

knowledge of magnetosphere dynamics (such as Chen et al. (2008) among countless oth- 122

ers), but a larger scale statistical study is needed in order to investigate broad multiscale 123

phenomena such as the connection between reconnection dynamics and global magne- 124

tosphere dynamics. Therefore, we have significant motivation to develop a machine learn- 125

ing model to improve upon existing plasmoid detection techniques. 126

2 Constructing perturbed magnetostatic equilibria 127

We wish to start our PIC simulations in hydrostatic equilibrium to avoid initially 128

injecting large amounts of energy into the simulation. The GS equation is a convenient 129

description of a 2D MHD equilibrium: 130

∇2Ay = −µ0 d dAy

Here we are assuming a geometry in which ˆy is the invariant direction. Ay is the ˆy com- 131

ponent of the magnetic vector potential, and is also known as the flux function in the 132

case of 2D plasma. Additionally, p is the gas pressure, By is the ˆy component of the mag- 133

netic field, and µ0 is the vacuum permeability. The GS equation is notably used in Grad- 134

Shafranov reconstruction, which is a method used to extrapolate the geometry of quasi- 135

magnetostatic, 2D structures from spacecraft data (Sonnerup et al., 2006). The solutions 136

of partial differential equations are not generally well behaved and will often exhibit bi- 137

furcations where a continuous change of parameters causes a discontinuous change in the 138

solution (Arnol’d, 1994). However, often a small perturbation of the right hand side (RHS) 139

of the equation will result in a solution which is qualitatively close to the unperturbed 140

analytic solution, and it is easy and quick to discard numeric solutions with differing be- 141

haviors via visual inspection. 142

The GS equation is a Poisson equation and therefore is solved as a boundary value 143

problem. This can cause problems when trying to numerically solve the GS equation in 144

space physics applications where the problem is unbounded or has boundary conditions 145

at infinity (such as the magnetic field vanishing there). There exist methods to impose 146

boundaries at infinity onto numerical solutions (Wang, 1999), though we do not use them 147

here for simplicity. In the context of solving the GS equation to find an approximate hy- 148

drostatic equilibrium which is close to a known analytic solution, we can impose finite 149

boundary conditions by requiring that the perturbed solution match the analytic one at 150

the boundary of the region of interest. It would also be possible to add further variabil- 151

ity to the solution by using boundary conditions which are slightly perturbed from the 152

analytic ones, but we have not explored this. 153

ris sheet for simplicity. Note also that if we were interested in the physics of reconnec- 159

tion onset it would be best to use the magnetotail-like configuration because having a 160

3 Example case: a simulated dataset for plasmoid detection 205

In this section, we continue our example of a potential use case for this method- 206

ology. We demonstrate the use of messy GS-constructed Harris-like equilibria as the start- 207

ing point of simulations of plasmoids in current sheets, and the use of said simulations 208

to train a simple plasmoid detection model. Our simulations are performed using the VPIC 209

particle-in-cell code (Bowers, Albright, Bergen, et al., 2008; Bowers, Albright, Yin, et 210

al., 2008; Bowers et al., 2009). Our 2D simulation space is a periodic 200di×50di box 211

where di is the ion inertial length, and the simulation runs for 60 ion cyclotron times. 212

We use an ion-to-electron mass ratio of 25, a cell size of 1.5 Debye lengths, and 600 plasma 213

particles per cell. We use a timestep that is 98% of the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy con- 214

dition in order to ensure numerical convergence while minimizing the number of timesteps 215

needed. The simulation uses a low plasma beta of 0.01, an electron velocity of 0.25c within 216

the sheet, and a cooler background plasma population which has an electron velocity of 217

0.15c. Ion and electron temperatures are kept equal. 218

We keep all plasma parameters the same in all simulations for this demonstrative 219

example, but models which will be applied to spacecraft data should be trained on sim- 220

ulations which have a broad spectrum of realistic plasma parameters. We elect to cre- 221

ate variations in the initial equilibrium conditions solely by deflecting the x coordinate 222

x →x + f(z) in the Harris sheet GS equation as described in Section 2.1. To choose 223

a somewhat random but continuous f(z) we use a Fourier series with 15 non-constant 224

terms: 225

While it would be possible to use the generated equilibria as initial conditions for 232

full 3D simulations, we elect to use simpler 2D simulations in order to simplify the con- 233

struction of our simulated dataset. In 2D, the magnetic topology contains unambigu- 234

ous magnetic nulls and separatrices which partition the plasma and provide definite bound- 235

aries for plasmoids. It is both possible and common to have multiple plasmoids contained 236

within another larger plasmoid, but the smaller-scale plasmoids are more of interest for 237

our goal of detecting plasmoids formed via the plasmoid instability in the magnetotail, 238

so we seek to label solely the innermost plasmoids for our dataset. A process for detect- 239

ing hierarchies of plasmoids is described in Banesh et al. (2020). 240

The first step towards finding plasmoids in the simulation is finding topological o- 241

points. Ignoring the potential constant guide field, magnetic nulls are places where both 242

in-plane components of the magnetic field Bz and Bx vanish. We find the locations of 243

these nulls by using the image processing library scikit-image (van der Walt et al., 2014) 244

to find the contours where Bz = 0 as well as the contours where Bx = 0, and then 245

locating their intersections. Gaussian filtering of the magnetic field data is first applied 246

to minimize numerical noise. We do not round the location of contour intersections to 247

the nearest grid point, instead using linear interpolation to calculate values away from 248

the simulation mesh. We next must determine whether the observed nulls are topolog- 249

ical o-points, which are defined as topological minima or maxima of the flux function Ay, 250

or topological x-points, which are saddles. We can determine this by taking the deter- 251

minant of the Hessian matrix H of Ay, which is defined as follows: 252

H = ∂xxAy ∂xzAy ∂zxAy ∂zzAy

 = ∂xBz −∂xBx ∂zBz −∂zBx

 ⇒det H = ∂xBx · ∂zBz −∂xBz · ∂zBx (6)

If det H is positive at a null point it is a topological o-point and if it is negative the null 253

point is a topological x-point (Hubbard & Hubbard, 2009). We categorize the null points 254

in our simulation in this fashion using numerical derivatives of the magnetic field com- 255

ponents. 256

The separatrices which separate plasmoids from the rest of the simulation origi- 257

nate at x-points and have constant Ay, so we can find them by tracing level contours of 258

Ay from each x-point. It is then straightforward to categorize all points surrounding an 259

o-point and bounded by separatrices as plasmoids. Now that we have established the ground 260

truth for our training, we assemble our spacecraft-like data by taking random 1D cuts 261

through the simulation, linearly interpolating to find values off the mesh. We first crop 262

the simulation to ±20de in the z direction to minimize the class imbalance between plas- 263

moid and non-plasmoid points. We then determine the location of the cuts by taking as 264

endpoints two random points within the cropped simulation space at a fixed time. The 265

possible segment lengths are limited to < 200di to shorten computation time. 100 seg- 266

ments are created from each time, and the times we use are spaced five ion cyclotron times 267

apart to ensure that the simulation has had time to evolve since the previous time slices 268

were taken. 269

3.1 Training a 1D CNN model 270

Now that we have our spacecraft-like data we are ready to train the model. The 271

prototypical model structure used for classification problems is a 2D Convolutional Neu- 272

ral Network (CNN) (O’Shea & Nash, 2015). Models based on this structure have achieved 273

excellent performance on classification tasks (e.g. Sharma et al., 2018). However, their 274

usage of 2D inputs would necessitate significant modification of the input data. Two po- 275

tential options directly suited to processing 1D data are Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) 276

and 1D CNNs. RNNs are better documented and are well-suited to data with a tempo- 277

ral component (Medsker & Jain, 1999). 1D CNNs generally require less computations 278

and have some recent evidence suggesting comparable performance to RNNs (Kiranyaz 279

et al., 2021). For the purposes of this example we have chosen to use a 1D CNN archi- 280

tecture. 281

Besides deciding on the model’s structure, we must also preprocess the data to be 282

in a suitable state for training. We did ten simulations, each starting from a different 283

perturbed equilibrium. To avoid cross contamination we use seven simulations exclusively 284

for training data and three exclusively for testing, a 70-30 training-testing split. We ad- 285

ditionally add to the training and testing dataset spacecraft-like data from a simulation 286

of a current sheet at the same parameters sans any plasmoids. Our goal is to be able to 287

predict if any given point in a spacecraft trajectory is inside of a plasmoid. The surround- 288

ing points and how the plasma parameters change there give some information about 289

the local plasma structure, so we include them in the model input. To increase the speed 290

of training, we configure the model to output predictions for 10 points simultaneously. 291

To standardize the size of the inputs to the ML model we use a sliding window to break 292

each ‘spacecraft trajectory’ into segments 30 datapoints in length. The model does the 293

prediction on the interior 10 points, using the exterior 20 for additional spatial informa- 294

tion. We next randomly shuffle all of the segments so that the model can’t pick up on 295

patterns based on the segments’ locations in the dataset. We then undersample the ma- 296

jority class of the training dataset (non-plasmoid points) by 85% to combat class imbal- 297

ance. After this process is done, we are left with 1170830 total points in the training dataset, 298

475718 non-plasmoid points and 695112 plasmoid points, a slight reversal of the imbal- 299

ance. The testing dataset, which was not undersampled, has 1684620 total points, 1320125 300

non-plasmoid and 364495 plasmoid, an imbalance of approximately 3.5:1. 301

There are several quantities commonly available from spacecraft which could be 302

fed to a ML model – some newer missions like MMS even provide electron and ion phase 303

space distribution functions (Pollock et al., 2016), which could be analyzed with 2D or 304

3D techniques (e.g. Olshevsky et al., 2021). For the purposes of this simple model, we 305

will use a handful which are directly correspond to our understanding of general traits 306

of plasmoids: Bx, By, Bz, jy (which is often but not always elevated within plasmoids), 307

and the plasma bulk velocity vz to quantify the direction the plasmoid is moving within 308

the sheet. Each quantity is passed through a convolutional and pooling layer to iden- 309

tify spatial features of interest. These data are then averaged together, then convolved 310

and pooled once more to select the most relevant features. A final fully connected layer 311

outputs ten logits which predict whether the ten central points of the inputted data seg- 312

ment are part of a plasmoid. More details are shown and discussed in Figure 3. 313

As this is merely an example model rather than a polished production one, we did 314

not aggressively optimize hyperparameters or otherwise maximize model performance. 315

We used cross entropy loss and the Adam optimizer, and only trained for ten epochs with 316

a learning rate of 0.01. Our training and testing performance is summarized in panel b) 317

of Figure 3. The model achieved a recall of 0.79 and a precision of 0.4 on the testing dataset, 318

meaning that 79% of the true positives were detected but only 40% of the predicted pos- 319

itives were actually positive. This is good recall, but the precision should be increased 320

to increase the model’s usability for scientific research. Additionally, good performance 321

on the synthesized dataset does not guarantee good performance on real spacecraft data. 322

A visualization of the model’s performance on some of our testing data is shown 323

in Figure 4, and it depicts a notable phenomenon. When describing our plasmoid-detection 324

process for the full 2D data, we noted that we would only find small-scale plasmoids us- 325

ing the method. Indeed, Figure 4 shows some structures which are clearly plasmoids by 326

visual inspection but are not flagged as such by our separatrix-based algorithm. Our ma- 327

chine learning model often identifies the cores of these plasmoids as plasmoids despite 328

the ground “truth” algorithm saying otherwise, which can be seen in the top panel of 329

*Figure 4. In a sense, for these plasmoids the ML model is “correct” and the separatrix- 330*

based algorithm is “incorrect”. This is not a rigorous test of the model’s capability, but 331

it gives reason for optimism. We describe our next steps in the final section. 332

4 Final Remarks 333

In this paper we have described a novel method to train ML models to detect plasma 334

structures in in-situ spacecraft data using simulated training data. Simulations are done 335

with ‘messy’ initial conditions created by tweaking the right hand side of the Grad-Shafranov 336

equation to better represent the variability of nature. Utilizing the complete informa- 337

tion known about the simulated system, the desired structures are located and labeled 338

in the simulation data. After this, 1D slices are taken from the simulations to replicate 339

spacecraft data. These slices then are used to train a supervised ML model to detect the 340

structures of interest. 341

We demonstrated the method by training a simple model to detect plasmoids in 342

spacecraft-like data. There is a need for this kind of model because current methods of 343

plasmoid detection are not well suited to detecting the large numbers of ‘messy’ plas- 344

moids necessary for a thorough statistical study of plasmoid impacts on turbulent mag- 345

netotail reconnection. These sorts of broad studies are necessary to develop an under- 346

standing of the overall characteristics of complex magnetotail reconnection and its in- 347

terplay with larger-scale magnetosphere processes like substorms, as well as multiscale 348

reconnection in large systems in general (Ji et al., 2022). 349

It will be necessary to develop a more sophisticated and better-performing model 350

than the simple 1D CNN shown here. Our simulations had scant reconnection and mostly 351

showed gradual evolution to a less perturbed state, so we will consider adding unsteady 352

and/or inhomogeneous driving to the simulation to encourage more dynamic evolution. 353

We could also attempt to fit the simulated plasmoids to cylindrical flux rope models such 354

as Lundquist (1950) or Elphic and Russell (1983) to quantify how much the “messy” plas- 355

moids deviate from the ideal. We intend to modify the separatrix-based plasmoid iden- 356

tification algorithm to detect interiors of large plasmoids, since not doing so is clearly 357

confusing our model. Hyperparameter optimization and postprocessing must be done 358

to combat the dataset’s imbalance. It also may be preferable to avoid training a model 359

from scratch and instead adapt an existing well-performing image classifier such as ResNet50 360

(He et al., 2015) which can be found pretrained online. In any case, after the model achieves 361

good performance on simulated data it will likely still perform poorly on real data due 362

to the many differences between our training data and real data, such as dimensional- 363

ity, sample rates, and sources of noise. To combat this we will utilize domain adapta- 364

tion, which is the process of modifying a model trained on one dataset so that it per- 365

forms well on another dataset. There are numerous existing methodologies which have 366

been developed to facilitate successful domain adaptation (Singhal et al., 2023). We are 367

currently using ADDA (Tzeng et al., 2017), to adapt simulation-trained models to MMS 368

data. This method uses adversarial training to extract the features from the target dataset 369

which are most similar to those identified in the source dataset, therefore excluding fea- 370

tures which differ between the two domains such as numerical noise. The shared features 371

from the target dataset are then used as input to the classifier model. We expect that 372

our results could be further improved by reducing the differences between the simulated 373

and real data, using methods similar to those employed by e.g. Tremblay et al. (2018), 374

but we have no plans of doing so at this time. We plan to evaluate the finished model’s 375

performance on a database of known magnetotail plasmoids such as e.g. Ieda et al. (1998). 376

It would also be beneficial to compare the model’s performance to potential alternate 377

models, such as ones which use training data that have synthetic instrument noise and 378

ones trained on unperturbed simulations or mathematical models. By comparing mul- 379

tiple approaches we can determine which factors are most important for training a suc- 380

cessful plasmoid detection model. 381

There are numerous potential applications of this process beyond the magnetotail 382

plasmoid detection model shown here. A logical extension would be to apply this pro- 383

cess to detect the plasmoids known as Flux Transfer Events (FTEs) which occur on Earth’s 384

dayside at the magnetopause; reconnection there is highly asymmetric so it would be in- 385

appropriate to simply use the model trained in this work. Magnetic structures are par- 386

ticularly hard to identify in turbulent plasmas, so this method could be used to identify 387

structures in reconnection outflows or in complex environments such as the turbulent 388

solar wind. For example, researchers looking for magnetic structures in Parker Solar Probe 389

data should consider this technique. 390
